newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn split on Europe credentials of French left.
newsitem.headline: Bonn split on Europe credentials of French left.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Monday he was convinced that, after Sunday's left-wing election victory in France, the new government would continue the country's support Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).

A senior ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl in the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), Peter Hintze, also said he was sure Paris would not alter its pro-European stance, but other politicians warned that a left-wing French government could jeopardise EMU.

Kinkel told reporters before a meeting of Free Democrat (FDP) party executives he was sure the planned single currency, the euro, would be launched on time and that countries participating would fulfil the criteria precisely.

"Germany and France remain for me the most important partners. We want to go further in Europe. The euro can be launched under strict adherence to the criteria and the planned timetable," Kinkel said.
CDU general secretary Hinzte said he hoped the new government would realise that launching EMU on time on a sound financial basis was in the interests of the whole of Europe.

"I am confident that the new French government will pursue a pro-European policy," Hintze said in a statement. "The launch of the euro on time is extremely important to Germany. We will make every effort to keep to the timetable."
In contrast, German newspapers voiced doubts and concerns about the future of Europe's integration drive, and especially its planned common currency, after the change of government in France.
Several commentaries noted the turn to the left in France, Germany's most important partner, was leaving Kohl increasingly isolated at a crucial time in the run-up to Europe's monetary union.

Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of the CDU's conservative Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, echoed commentators' doubts and said the change of government in France could put European integration at risk.
"The French left will be reliant on the support of the communists, who call into question further integration in Europe with their rejection of European curreny union," Glos said in a statement.
Kinkel said that although Franco-German partnership was still the chief motor behind European economic union, the two countries might have different views on some issues.
